entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA states it can serve more than 100% of demand, or data-centre revenue falls sequentially, for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Buyers order more accelerators than NVIDIA can build, so orders queue up and sales are set by what the factories release rather than by what customers want.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging output, since supply rather than orders sets the revenue line.
entries.statement: Datacenter GPU demand continues to outrun NVIDIA's ability to serve it.
entries.title: NVDA demand durability

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Stacked-memory lead times fall to available-on-demand and advanced-packaging lead times drop below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
entries.mechanism: Every accelerator needs both stacked memory and advanced packaging, so the scarcer of the two sets the ceiling on how many can be built.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new memory fabs and packaging lines come online relative to accelerator orders.
entries.statement: Memory and advanced packaging are both capping how much merchant-GPU vendors can ship, with high-bandwidth memory sold out through 2027 and TSMC packaging booked out at 52 to 78 week lead times even as capacity climbs toward 130,000 wafers a month.
entries.title: Supply constraint binding

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's accelerator share fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
entries.mechanism: AMD wins named commitments and ships racks, but its deliveries arrive later than the commitments, so its share of installed accelerators lags its order announcements.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the 2027 volume ramp lands on schedule.
entries.statement: AMD's data-center sales nearly doubled to $6.7 billion in the second quarter of 2026 and its Helios racks are in production with Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Microsoft named, yet its accelerator share stays near 5 to 10 percent against NVIDIA at roughly 90 percent because volume shipments only ramp through 2027.
entries.title: AMD credible second source

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Custom-chip share growth falls back below merchant accelerator growth for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Cloud buyers build their own chips for steady inference work, but their overall compute needs are growing faster than their in-house lines can fill, so they keep buying merchant parts as well.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether in-house chips reach volume production on their stated 2027 and 2028 dates.
entries.statement: Hyperscaler custom silicon meaningfully displaces merchant-GPU demand growth.
entries.title: Custom ASIC substitution

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Published rental rates for a current-generation part drop more than 20% within a quarter.
entries.mechanism: Scarce new capacity keeps published hourly rates firm, while second-hand card prices fall as more used stock reaches the market.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much prior-generation capacity is freed up as new racks are installed.
entries.statement: Published rental rates for current and prior generation accelerators are holding or edging up while used-card asking prices have drifted below their earlier peaks.
entries.title: Pricing power persistence

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Policy eases enough that China data-centre revenue recovers above prior levels within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rules on both sides of the Pacific decide which buyers may take delivery, so policy sets the size of the market before any commercial negotiation starts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the drafted rental rule and tariff framework are published in binding form.
entries.statement: Export-control policy materially constrains addressable merchant-GPU demand.
entries.title: Export control exposure

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed accelerator commitments exceed 300,000 units within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the seller guarantees the buyer's leases or credit, reported orders partly reflect the seller's own balance sheet rather than independent purchasing power.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the third-party financing platforms convert from non-binding memorandums into funded deals.
entries.statement: NVIDIA still underwrites a large share of its own demand through site lease guarantees and outside investor money, having cut one customer guarantee from $250 billion to under $120 billion, capped a new site guarantee at $105 billion, signed platforms meant to raise over $500 billion from third parties, and now paused some deals under a compute-partnership programme carrying $36 billion of six-year commitments, which NVIDIA denies is halted.
entries.title: Vendor-financed demand circularity

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's quarterly filing shows every direct customer below 15% of total revenue, down from the disclosed 21%, 17% and 16%, for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A handful of buyers account for most of the order book, so one of them slowing down removes a large slice of demand at once.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the financial health of the single largest committed tenant.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's data-center revenue is increasingly concentrated in a few direct customers, raising demand-durability risk if any single hyperscaler slows orders or shifts to in-house silicon.
entries.title: Customer concentration risk

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA slips from the number 1 spot in data-centre Ethernet switching within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Selling the switching fabric with the accelerators means a buyer who swaps vendors has to requalify the whole cluster, not just the chips.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether large buyers start pairing rival accelerators with standard switching.
entries.statement: NVIDIA now leads the data-center Ethernet switch market and sells that networking bundled with its GPUs, deepening a full-system moat that raises switching costs versus standalone accelerators and custom chips. NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in data-center Ethernet switching in Q1 2026 by pairing Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300, and its NVLink systems cut cost per token, but no finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the sharper claim that networking scales faster than compute is not supported.
entries.title: Networking attach as systems moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so token economics improve less than one generation cycle.
entries.mechanism: Each generation cuts the cost of serving a request, which makes applications that were too expensive to run worth running and adds to total demand.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rising memory costs cancel out the per-request savings.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's each-generation drop in cost per token pulls more inference workloads onto its GPUs and widens the market it can serve.
entries.title: Cheaper inference pulls in demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid memory commitments shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
entries.mechanism: Customers who put cash down years ahead for memory have already paid for the accelerators that memory will go into, which makes those orders hard to cancel.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether new take-or-pay agreements keep being signed at the same size.
entries.statement: Non-cancelable multi-year HBM contracts backed by billions in customer deposits lock a large share of future accelerator demand into place and reduce the chance that today's buildout is speculative.
entries.title: Prepaid HBM take-or-pay locks in accelerator demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Policy changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear the current flagship within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Washington caps what may be licensed and Beijing discourages what is licensed from crossing the border, so approved volumes never turn into shipped revenue.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether Beijing lets licensed hardware enter the mainland.
entries.statement: China's reopening to NVIDIA is now blocked from both sides, with Washington allowing only case-by-case licences under a sub-50 percent cap and a 25 percent tariff while Beijing tells approved buyers to keep the licensed hardware in Hong Kong to protect its own chipmakers, so shipments stay trivial and no revenue has yet been booked.
entries.title: Conditional China re-opening with a capped ceiling

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD or non-NVIDIA designWins in production inference keep expanding for two consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rival software stacks have improved enough that the largest buyers now run production work on non-NVIDIA chips, so software difficulty no longer holds them in place.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the announced gigawatt commitments actually run production traffic rather than staying pilots.
entries.statement: The difficulty of running existing AI software on non-Nvidia chips keeps customers on Nvidia even when rivals cut hardware prices.
entries.title: CUDA software lock-in sustains the moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Memory capacity expansion pulls standard memory and flash prices down within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Memory is a large and rising share of what an AI server costs, so its price sets the bill of materials and then the selling price.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new memory fabs reach volume output.
entries.statement: Memory and flash prices keep raising what every AI server costs, with component waits of 32 to 40 weeks, memory prices up about 90 percent since late 2025 and contract prices up roughly 50 percent this year, and the leading vendor is now passing more than 15 percent of that increase into system prices from early next year rather than leaving it all on system builders' margins, while the largest contract builder still reports that high memory prices have not slowed customer spending.
entries.title: Rising memory costs inflate AI-server economics

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Schedule slips push a major vendor's second-half 2026 ramp into 2027.
entries.mechanism: Each vendor's ramp depends on its own memory and packaging slots, so their production dates spread out instead of landing together.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory qualification timing on each vendor's newest part.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's newest racks ramp into production from the third quarter of 2026 while AMD's rack-scale volume mostly arrives in 2027, so the multi-vendor supply wave lands in stages rather than all at once. Supply-chain reporting still has NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google parts entering mass production together and AMD's rack reached production with third-quarter shipments, but one account puts AMD's real volume ramp and first production output at the second quarter of 2027 because of manufacturing delays, and Meta's in-house parts only enter production in September.
entries.title: Multi-vendor accelerator supply wave in second-half 2026

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's buyer base broadens so customer concentration eases over the next 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A few very large agreements carry most of the growth, so one partner changing plans moves AMD's whole accelerator line.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the named gigawatt partners keep to their deployment schedules.
entries.statement: AMD's data-center accelerator growth depends on a small set of very large commitments, which concentrates both its upside and its downside in a handful of partners.
entries.title: AMD growth leans on a few mega-deals

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island slips its customer sampling past the second-half 2026 quarter.
entries.mechanism: Using ordinary low-power memory instead of stacked memory takes the part out of the queue for the scarcest components.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the cheaper memory is fast enough for real inference workloads.
entries.statement: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to sidestep the advanced-packaging and memory bottleneck, opening an alternative supply route for inference chips.
entries.title: Memory-based inference chips route around the packaging bottleneck

entries.falsifiableTrigger: TSMC's gross margin declines for 2 consecutive quarters as capacity loosens.
entries.mechanism: Demand from accelerators, custom chips, networking and power parts all lands on the same production lines, so the queue lengthens and the foundry can charge more.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much work moves to rival packaging suppliers.
entries.statement: AI demand spreading across GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips fills TSMC's capacity across nodes and lets it raise prices.
entries.title: Broadening AI demand tightens TSMC capacity and pricing

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscaler cuts its 2026 or 2027 AI capital spending guidance within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Spending is committed years ahead of the revenue it is meant to earn, so any shortfall in returns shows up first as cancelled or deferred orders.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest model buyers can keep raising outside capital.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' sharp jump in AI capital spending risks a pullback if returns disappoint, which would cut accelerator orders.
entries.title: Hyperscaler AI spending may outrun near-term returns

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's gross margin guidance drops below 70% in a coming quarter.
entries.mechanism: Memory is bought at rising prices and only part of the increase is passed through to system prices, so the difference comes out of the margin.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the memory increase customers accept in system prices.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's gross margin is stepping down from 75% toward a stated floor of 71% to 72%, with 74% guided for the coming quarter, because memory costs are rising faster than the company expected, so the premium is now being partly given back to its suppliers.
entries.title: NVIDIA holds a premium gross margin as it ramps new chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer concentration in advanced-packaging output falls below 85% within a year.
entries.mechanism: Because so few customers hold the bookings, capacity freed by any one of them cannot easily be sold to anyone else.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether smaller chip designers win packaging slots as new lines open.
entries.statement: A few AI chip buyers control most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one of them cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
entries.title: AI packaging supply is concentrated in a few buyers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate order-book duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Scarcity pushes buyers to lock in future output, which stretches the average life of the order book.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether supply loosens enough that buyers no longer need to book years ahead.
entries.statement: Cloud and chip suppliers are signing longer-dated purchase commitments that push out the average life of their order books, so a growing share of AI compute demand is booked years in advance.
entries.title: Backlog duration lengthens as demand is booked years ahead

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
entries.mechanism: Rising sales at the model providers give the buildout a real revenue base, but commitments are still signed ahead of the cash those sales produce.

pendingChallenge.rationale: SpaceX's AI revenue reached $2.6 billion, up 247% year over year, but the largest committed tenant is unprofitable and seeking over $500 billion of outside capital, and Anthropic's run of very large commitments in about eight months is read as labs having ample financing to buy ahead of revenue rather than paying out of sales.

entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether reported annualised revenue converts into cash that funds the commitments.
entries.statement: Leading AI model providers are growing revenue fast enough that their heavy compute spending rests on real and rising sales rather than hope.
entries.title: Model-provider revenue scales to underpin the buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator design wins for frontier training stall over the next 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Policy shelters domestic accelerator makers from foreign competition, which lets them grow revenue even where their parts are not yet equal to the alternatives.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic suppliers can obtain enough stacked memory.
entries.statement: China's home-grown accelerators can now train frontier-scale models without NVIDIA chips, but Chinese buyers still order far more NVIDIA parts than are available, so the displacement is proven in capability and not yet in volume. Two findings show a 1.6-trillion-parameter model pretrained on more than 50,000 domestic accelerators across over 35 trillion tokens, while Chinese firms ordered more than two million restricted NVIDIA parts for 2026 against roughly 700,000 units of inventory and domestic labs' own chips are judged more than two years away.
entries.title: China Domestic Accelerators Displace Banned NVIDIA GPUs

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's debt load or net loss narrows for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: These operators buy hardware years before the rental income arrives, so faster growth means larger upfront costs before any profit.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly newly bought fleets fill with paying customers.
entries.statement: Fast-growing neocloud GPU buyers such as CoreWeave are booking record revenue while their net losses widen.
entries.title: Neocloud GPU Buyers Grow Revenue but Deepen Losses

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
entries.mechanism: Electricity and site readiness decide how many racks can be switched on, so power caps deployment even when hardware is available.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to grid connection timelines at the largest new campuses.
entries.statement: Companies now size and cap their AI buildouts by gigawatts of available power, so electricity and site capacity increasingly limit how many accelerators they can actually deploy.
entries.title: Power capacity is becoming the binding limit on AI buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The two incumbents' combined share of custom design work falls below 90% within a year.
entries.mechanism: As more design houses win custom-chip work, the alternative to merchant accelerators stops depending on any single pair of suppliers.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the newer entrants actually ship volume on their stated dates.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' shift to custom AI chips runs almost entirely through two outside design firms, so the alternative to merchant GPUs is itself concentrated in those two suppliers.
entries.title: The custom-AI-chip alternative depends on two design houses

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Wistron's monthly AI-related revenue falls year over year for 2 consecutive months.
entries.mechanism: Contract builders only book revenue when finished systems leave the factory, so their monthly sales track real shipments rather than announcements.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to component shortages that hold finished systems on the line.
entries.statement: Contract server makers post record monthly revenue as AI-server and networking orders ship in volume.
entries.title: ODM AI-server revenue confirms real shipments

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's debt-to-equity ratio rises above 6:1 within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Borrowing against hardware that has not yet earned rental income leaves a thin equity cushion if utilisation or rates fall.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether lease income from anchor tenants covers the debt service.
entries.statement: Neocloud operators fund their GPU fleets mostly with debt, leaving thin equity cushions.
entries.title: Neocloud GPU buyers carry heavy debt loads

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
entries.mechanism: Putting the optics into the switch package cuts power and parts count but ties cluster wiring to a narrow set of packaging and laser suppliers.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to optical engine yields at the few qualified suppliers.
entries.statement: The move to co-packaged optics is reshaping how AI networking gear is built and supplied, tying cluster wiring to a fast-changing optics roadmap.
entries.title: Optical networking shifts to co-packaged optics as a supply lever

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A named US fabrication or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
entries.mechanism: New domestic plants add capacity that does not depend on a single island, which widens the base of suppliers over time.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to construction and qualification timelines, since the memory packaging plant only reaches production in 2029.
entries.statement: NVIDIA and its partners are committing to build AI hardware inside the United States at very large scale, adding fabrication and packaging capacity outside Taiwan.
entries.title: US onshoring broadens the AI hardware supply base

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave order books fail to grow sequentially for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Deliverable capacity lags signed contracts, so the order book shows demand earlier than reported sales do.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the next round of cloud results discloses order-book totals.
entries.statement: Cloud providers are booking compute contracts far faster than they can deliver them, so their reported backlogs now show demand better than their quarterly sales do.
entries.title: Cloud backlog conversion becomes the demand proof point

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capital guidance for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Spending is running ahead of what the businesses earn, so the gap is filled with borrowed or raised money, sometimes through a leasing partner rather than the buyer's own balance sheet.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the next round of cloud cash-flow disclosures.
entries.statement: The largest cloud buyers are turning to debt and share issuance to pay for AI capacity instead of funding it from cash generated by their businesses.
entries.title: Hyperscalers now borrow to fund the buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x efficiency gain over its predecessor.
entries.mechanism: More work per watt lets a fixed power budget carry more useful capacity, which softens the effect of power and packaging caps.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether vendor efficiency claims hold up in customer deployments.
entries.statement: Each new generation of AI racks does far more work per megawatt, which lets buyers add capacity even when power and packaging are capped.
entries.title: Efficiency gains stretch scarce power and packaging

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Stacked-memory lead times shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for 2 consecutive quarters before the end of 2027.
entries.mechanism: Stacked memory takes about three times the wafer area of ordinary memory and cannot be substituted, so its output sets how many accelerators can be finished.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to stacking yields on the newest memory and to how much wafer capacity is diverted to it.
entries.statement: Stacked memory, not chips or packaging alone, now decides how many accelerators NVIDIA and AMD can actually deliver.
entries.title: Memory supply is the new choke point on accelerator shipments

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier gross margins fall for 2 consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
entries.mechanism: Memory suppliers set prices in a shortage while system vendors can only pass part of the increase through, so the profit shifts upstream.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the memory increase system buyers accept.
entries.statement: Memory suppliers are earning extraordinary margins on AI parts, shifting profit from the server builders toward the memory makers.
entries.title: Memory makers capture a growing share of AI server profit

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 accelerators is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Governments and large enterprises now buy whole clusters directly, which adds a demand tier that does not depend on the cloud giants' budgets.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to public funding decisions and to whether these buyers get allocation ahead of the big clouds.
entries.statement: National projects and large enterprises are now placing accelerator orders big enough to matter alongside the cloud giants.
entries.title: Sovereign and enterprise buyers become a new demand tier

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-centre revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Better yields and higher prices lift both the chip and the foundry businesses, which puts a third supplier back into data-centre supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether external foundry customers move from commitments to volume orders.
entries.statement: Intel's data-center and foundry businesses are growing again with better margins, adding a third source of AI-adjacent supply.
entries.title: Intel returns as a data-center supplier

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new vendor equity-for-compute deal appears for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors put their own money into the firms that buy from them, so reported demand partly reflects capital the seller supplied.

pendingChallenge.rationale: No new equity-for-compute deal with a chip customer appeared this cycle, and reporting says NVIDIA has paused certain deals under the compute-partnership programme that carried $36 billion of commitments, with internal staff raising antitrust concerns and partners objecting to restrictions, though NVIDIA denies the programme is halted; the same period saw it cut a customer guarantee from $250 billion to under $120 billion.

entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to outside investors replacing vendor money in these deals.
entries.statement: Merchant accelerator vendors are now buying equity stakes in the AI firms that buy their chips, tying reported demand to vendor-funded customers beyond NVIDIA alone.
entries.title: chipmakers take equity in their own customers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Standard memory spot prices fall for 2 consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
entries.mechanism: Every wafer turned into stacked memory is a wafer not turned into ordinary memory, so shortage and price rises spread to everything else that uses it.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the ratio of wafer capacity suppliers allocate to stacked memory.
entries.statement: The stacked-memory shortage is spreading into standard memory and raising prices on consumer and general-purpose graphics parts.
entries.title: memory crunch spills into consumer and general-purpose parts

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for 2 consecutive quarters through 2027.
entries.mechanism: Buying memory output years ahead moves a vendor to the front of the allocation queue when supply is short.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these partnerships convert from letters of intent into signed supply contracts.
entries.statement: Accelerator makers are signing multi-year partnerships and joint development deals straight with memory suppliers to reserve future stacked-memory output.
entries.title: Chip vendors buy their memory supply directly

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's stacked-memory share falls below 50% within 4 quarters as rivals ship volume.
entries.mechanism: Once a second supplier reaches comparable yields, buyers can qualify it and the leader's control over who gets memory fades.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the challenger's parts pass customer qualification.
entries.statement: One supplier holds most of the stacked-memory market and the largest cloud buyers have locked up long-term contracts, so access to that single source now decides who can build AI servers.
entries.title: Stacked-memory supply sits with one dominant maker

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or approved-buyer list reduction is reported for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Prosecutions raise the cost of physically diverting hardware, but renting compute offshore leaves no shipment to seize, so the second route stays open until a rule covers it.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the drafted offshore-rental rule is published and survives legal challenge.
entries.statement: Prosecutions and shorter approved-buyer lists are closing the smuggling route into China, but renting banned hardware offshore remains an open channel that regulators have only just begun to investigate.
entries.title: Enforcement closes the gray route into China

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Advanced-packaging lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
entries.mechanism: Packaging capacity can be added by building lines and outsourcing steps, while memory capacity needs new fabs, so the two constraints ease on different clocks.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much front-end packaging work moves to outside assembly partners.
entries.statement: Advanced packaging capacity keeps expanding but reports now disagree on whether the shortfall has narrowed to about 10 percent or is still near 20 percent, with lines booked through 2027, while memory shows no easing at all.
entries.title: Packaging tightness starts to ease while memory does not

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Flash contract prices for server drives fall for 2 consecutive quarters while the newest generation keeps deploying.
entries.mechanism: The newest racks add a large drive tier, so each system pulls far more flash than the previous generation did.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the announced flash capacity investments actually receive their public support.
entries.statement: The newest accelerator generation adds a large storage tier that is pulling flash demand up sharply and is already showing up as rising server costs.
entries.title: Storage becomes the next scarce part in the AI rack

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Every major cloud provider publishes list rates for its newest rack-scale systems for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the newest capacity is fully committed to contracts, providers stop listing a public rate for it and quote through sales instead.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much newest-generation capacity is left over after contracted customers are served.
entries.statement: Some cloud providers now quote their newest rack systems only through sales while others still publish rates for the same class of hardware, so public price pages show only part of what leading-edge capacity costs.
entries.title: The newest systems leave the public price list

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's accelerator share stabilises or rises for 2 consecutive quarters while rival shipments grow.
entries.mechanism: Rivals can only take share if their shipments grow faster than the leader's, and this cycle the leader's shipments accelerated.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the market rival racks reach in 2027.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's share of AI accelerators is falling even as its revenue sets records, so rivals are taking growth rather than taking business away.
entries.title: NVIDIA's share slips while its sales still grow

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer returns to purchasing loose accelerators rather than vendor racks for a flagship cluster within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors now sell the accelerators, networking and software as one unit, so buyers compare complete racks and cannot mix parts freely.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether open rack standards let buyers assemble their own systems.
entries.statement: Both merchant vendors now sell whole 72-accelerator racks with their own networking and software rather than individual chips, so buyers compare complete systems instead of parts.
entries.title: The rack, not the chip, is now the unit of competition

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Texas data-centre power additions exceed 5 GW over the next 4 quarters as the pause lifts.
entries.mechanism: A site cannot open until the grid connects it, so the connection queue rather than chip supply sets the opening date.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to state-level connection policy and to whether utility investment brings new generation online.
entries.statement: New AI sites are held up mainly by grid connection queues and state-level pauses rather than by chip supply, with a Texas connection queue of roughly 474 gigawatts where about 90 percent of requests are data centres yet only about 1.2 gigawatts of additions are forecast over the next year and up to $8 billion of lost data-centre revenue attributed to the pause; no finding this cycle reports transformer lead times.
entries.title: Grid equipment lead times gate new AI sites

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Median newest-generation rental rates fall while prior-generation rates rise for 2 consecutive months.
entries.mechanism: Buyers pay up for whatever just launched because it is scarce, while older parts compete against each other and their quotes spread out.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly newest-generation capacity reaches the public rental market.
entries.statement: Rental prices for the newest systems are rising while quotes for the previous generation spread out and drift lower, so the price premium is concentrating in whatever just launched.
entries.title: The rental premium moves to the newest hardware

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Alternative packaging lead times rise above 52 weeks, or no accelerator maker places advanced-packaging volume outside TSMC for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the leading packager is booked out, chip designers qualify second sources that quote shorter waits, and work follows the shorter queue.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the alternative routes hit their 2027 production targets at usable yields.
entries.statement: Accelerator makers are starting to route advanced-packaging work to Samsung, Amkor, ASE and Intel because those suppliers quote far shorter waits than TSMC.
entries.title: Packaging work starts to spread beyond TSMC

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's share of advanced-packaging output rises above 15% within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A fixed allocation must be divided between two product lines, so every processor packaged displaces an accelerator.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AMD secures slots at alternative packaging suppliers.
entries.statement: AMD holds only about a tenth of TSMC's advanced-packaging output and must split it between its server processors and its accelerators, so every processor it packages costs it an accelerator.
entries.title: AMD's packaging slots force a product trade-off

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The next flagship ships with its originally planned 288GB memory configuration within 2 quarters of launch.
entries.mechanism: Putting less memory on each accelerator lets a fixed pool of memory cover more units, so the product shrinks instead of the volume.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to stacking yields on the taller memory stacks.
entries.statement: NVIDIA is cutting the memory in its next top-end accelerator to 192 gigabytes, far below the one terabyte it previewed and below the 288 gigabytes of the current generation, because it cannot secure enough stacked memory and because sites cannot supply enough power.
entries.title: Memory shortage now shrinks the product, not just the volume

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The first Korean AI factory misses its 2027 target or the partnership is not converted from letters of intent into signed contracts within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Tying memory supply, site construction and cloud capacity to one national group concentrates a second cluster of the buildout in that country.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the letters of intent become binding contracts.
entries.statement: NVIDIA and one Korean group have tied together data-centre construction, memory supply and cloud capacity in a partnership described as more than $500 billion, making Korea a second hub of the buildout alongside the United States.
entries.title: Korea becomes a second centre of the AI buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No accelerator or system vendor announces a shipping product using the high-bandwidth flash specification within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A standard flash tier gives system designers a cheaper memory layer that does not draw on the same scarce stacked-memory supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether an accelerator vendor actually designs the new tier into a shipping product.
entries.statement: The industry has published a first standard for a high-bandwidth flash tier and is designing racks around large drive pools, creating a cheaper memory layer that does not compete for scarce stacked-memory supply.
entries.title: Flash steps in where stacked memory runs out

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD software releases deliver less than a 1.5x measured inference gain over the prior release for 2 consecutive releases.
entries.mechanism: Software speedups apply to hardware already installed, so they lift AMD's competitiveness before its new racks reach volume.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether independent testing confirms the vendor's own performance claims.
entries.statement: AMD is reporting large software-driven speedups on its current accelerators, which lifts its competitiveness now even though its new racks do not ship in volume until 2027.
entries.title: AMD's software gains arrive ahead of its volume

entries.falsifiableTrigger: SpaceX nameplate compute fails to exceed 2 gigawatts by the end of 2026 or its quarterly AI capital spending falls below $10 billion for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A single privately funded buyer scaling this fast takes a large slice of one vendor's output, which reshapes who gets allocation.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether its AI revenue keeps funding capital spending at this rate.
entries.statement: SpaceX has built its compute fleet from 400 megawatts to 1.4 gigawatts in a year, spent $15.8 billion on AI infrastructure in a single quarter, and says it will build exclusively on NVIDIA while expecting a very significant share of NVIDIA's 2027 output.
entries.title: A rocket company becomes a top-tier accelerator buyer

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Intel's share of 2.5D packaging capacity fails to rise above 20% within 4 quarters, or its bridge packaging misses 2027 mass production.
entries.mechanism: The alternative route depends on one capacitor supplier and one substrate ramp, so its own narrowest link caps how much work it can absorb.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to substrate yields and to whether a second capacitor supplier is qualified.
entries.statement: Intel's bridge packaging is winning volume orders, but a single supplier of its silicon capacitors is already fully booked and the technology is described as a better fit for custom chips than for high-bandwidth accelerators.
entries.title: The alternative packaging route has its own choke point

entries.falsifiableTrigger: MediaTek's share of AI accelerators fails to exceed 5% within 4 quarters, or its first chip misses fourth-quarter 2026 production.
entries.mechanism: A third design house with funded capacity and named cloud customers gives buyers another route to custom silicon.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether its first part reaches production on the fourth-quarter 2026 date.
entries.statement: MediaTek has raised its accelerator share target to 15-20% and puts its first chip into production in the fourth quarter of 2026, adding a third supplier to a custom-chip design market that two firms had to themselves.
entries.title: A third designer enters the custom AI chip business

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Used prior-generation server prices fall more than 40% within 2 quarters, or published prior-generation rental rates drop below $2.00 per accelerator-hour.
entries.mechanism: Older machines cost a fraction of new ones while still earning rental income, so buyers keep them running rather than retiring them.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much prior-generation stock is freed up as new racks are installed.
entries.statement: A new top-end server costs about $500,000 against roughly $150,000 to $180,000 for a used prior-generation one, and rental rates for the same card range from $1.42 to $4.50 an hour, so older hardware keeps earning its place.
entries.title: Prior-generation systems stay in service on price

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Wafer suppliers report spare 300mm capacity or falling wafer prices for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: New memory and packaging plants all draw on the same blank wafers, so the squeeze moves one step further back up the chain.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how many new memory fabs come online at once in 2027.
entries.statement: Silicon wafer makers are running their lines at full utilisation, prices are rising and buyers are signing decade-long deals, so the squeeze now reaches one step further back than memory itself.
entries.title: Silicon wafer supply tightens behind the memory crunch

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's reported remaining performance obligations stay below $1 billion for 2 consecutive quarters while new gigawatt commitments keep being announced.
entries.mechanism: Announced gigawatt intentions do not become contracted obligations until orders are placed, so the reported obligation figure is the honest measure of what is firm.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the named partners convert intent into purchase orders in 2027.
entries.statement: AMD has announced multi-gigawatt customer commitments while reporting only $222 million of contracted obligations beyond one year, so most of its pipeline is still intent rather than firm order.
entries.title: AMD's announced gigawatt deals are not yet booked orders

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No hardwired inference product reaches customer shipment within 4 quarters, or inference workloads stay on general accelerators for 2 consecutive quarters after launch.
entries.mechanism: Chips built for one finished model run it far more cheaply than a general accelerator, so cost-sensitive inference work can move off merchant parts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how often models change, since rewiring silicon for each new model is expensive.
entries.statement: Accelerator vendors are buying startups that burn model weights straight into silicon, a cheaper approach to running finished models that could take work away from general-purpose accelerators.
entries.title: Hardwired inference chips emerge as a new rival to general accelerators

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Non-cloud owners stop signing new rental or lease agreements for 2 consecutive quarters, or the rented share of their fleets falls below 50%.
entries.mechanism: Owners who bought more capacity than they can use themselves rent the surplus out, which adds a layer of supply between chip vendors and end users.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these owners' own workloads grow enough to absorb their fleets.
entries.statement: Companies that bought accelerators for their own use are now renting much of that capacity to others, adding a new layer of supply between the chip vendors and end users.
entries.title: Compute owners outside the big clouds start renting capacity out

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Reported HBM4 yields fall back below 70% or contract prices keep rising for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Better yield only helps if wafer capacity is available, and stacked memory consumes three to four times the wafers of standard memory, so higher yields have not translated into more delivered supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to wafer allocation rather than yield, since wafer supply is now the limiting factor.
entries.statement: Both large Korean memory makers have pushed yields on the newest stacked memory to about 80 percent, months ahead of plan, which points to more supply reaching accelerator makers than today's sold-out order books imply.
entries.title: Memory yields improve fast enough to promise relief

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No compute-financing platform closes a funded transaction within 2 quarters, or the memorandums lapse without binding agreements.
entries.mechanism: Moving the funding onto outside investors takes the purchase off the vendor's and the cloud's balance sheets, which lets more hardware be bought per dollar of their own capital.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the non-binding memorandums turn into funded deals.
entries.statement: Large asset managers and banks are being lined up to finance accelerator purchases, moving part of the buildout's funding from chip vendors and cloud balance sheets onto third-party capital.
entries.title: Outside investors start funding the compute buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Samsung foundry utilisation loosens or it reverses the 10-15% price increase within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the leading foundry is full, work spills to the second source, which fills up in turn and gains room to raise prices.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether spillover demand persists once the leader adds capacity.
entries.statement: Samsung's contract chipmaking business is now full enough that it raised prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders and cannot meet all the orders it receives, so AI demand is tightening capacity beyond the market leader.
entries.title: The second-largest foundry fills up and raises prices

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Cerebras fails to report CS-4 customer shipments within 2 quarters, or no named customer expands beyond its initial system within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Designing the system to hand work to rival racks lets it be added to existing clusters instead of having to replace them.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether named customers place repeat orders.
entries.statement: Cerebras is shipping a rack-scale system built from three whole-wafer processors with named cloud and research customers, and it plugs into rival vendors' racks rather than replacing them outright.
entries.title: Wafer-scale machines join the rack contest

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new vendor-guaranteed or vendor-funded data-centre site above 1 gigawatt is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: If no powered site exists, the hardware cannot be installed, so the vendor funds the sites to create places for its own products to go.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much balance-sheet risk the vendor is willing to carry, given it already cut one guarantee.
entries.statement: The leading accelerator vendor is now guaranteeing data-centre leases and investing in powered land so that sites exist for its own hardware to fill.
entries.title: Chip vendors start buying the land and power behind their customers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscaler raises AI capital guidance and its shares rise on the day for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Investors read a bigger capital budget as cash going out now against uncertain returns later, so they mark down whoever is doing the spending.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether reported returns on earlier spending improve; only one finding this cycle bears on it.
entries.statement: Shares fall on the day a company raises its own capital spending whether it is a cloud buyer or a chip supplier, as when AMD's stock dropped more than 8% because its quarterly capital spending of $808 million came in well above the roughly $298 million expected.
entries.title: Investors now treat bigger AI budgets as a cost

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Capacitor lead times for AI server grades fall below 20 weeks for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A server cannot ship without every part on its bill of materials, so a cheap component in short supply stops an expensive machine.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast passive-component makers add capacity.
entries.statement: Waits for the small high-specification capacitors that every AI server needs are stretching toward 40 weeks, so shortages now reach parts that cost pennies as well as the expensive chips.
entries.title: Passive parts join the AI server shortage list

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new trading-firm compute commitment above $1 billion is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Trading firms buy compute for their own models and rent rather than build, which adds a buyer group outside the clouds and the model labs.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to trading-firm profitability, which funds these commitments.
entries.statement: Financial trading firms are now signing multi-billion-dollar capacity deals with specialist compute providers, adding a buyer group that sits outside both the cloud giants and the model builders.
entries.title: Trading firms become a new class of accelerator renter

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The next flagship launches in a single memory configuration, or the number of assessed memory specifications falls below 2 within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: When neither memory nor site power is guaranteed, the vendor hedges by preparing several versions so it can build whichever inputs arrive.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory qualification results on the taller stacks.
entries.statement: NVIDIA is preparing its next flagship in several memory and power versions at once rather than one configuration, so scarcity is splitting a single product into a family.
entries.title: One flagship becomes several part numbers under scarcity

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major vendor's next flagship arrives more than 24 months after its predecessor, or a named 2027 or 2028 roadmap part slips by 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors shorten the gap between generations to keep the performance lead, so buyers face a new top-end system roughly every year.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory and packaging can qualify fast enough to support annual launches.
entries.statement: Accelerator vendors are compressing the gap between generations, so buyers face a new top-end system roughly every year instead of every two to three.
entries.title: Product cycles get shorter

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No model builder taped out a custom accelerator within 4 quarters, or the announced design effort is abandoned within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Labs with steady, well-understood inference workloads can justify designing a chip for that one job rather than paying for a general accelerator.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these new designs can obtain stacked memory in an already short market.
entries.statement: The companies that build the largest models are moving from buying chips to designing them, adding a new source of custom silicon beyond the cloud giants.
entries.title: Model builders start designing their own chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The announced system price increase above 15% is withdrawn or rack quotes fall for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Memory is a large part of the bill of materials, so a sustained price rise has to show up either in the selling price or in the margin.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers accept the higher system prices without cutting volume.
entries.statement: The leading vendor is raising prices on AI server systems by more than 15% for shipments from early next year as memory costs climb.
entries.title: Chip vendors pass memory costs into system prices

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Mid-size cloud AI contract signings fall or capital spending drops below 20% of revenue for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Customers shut out of the largest clouds sign long contracts with smaller providers, which then spend a large share of revenue building the capacity to serve them.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these providers can fund capacity ahead of the contract revenue.
entries.statement: Smaller cloud providers are signing multi-year compute contracts worth hundreds of millions and spending a third of their revenue on capacity to serve them.
entries.title: Mid-size clouds win multi-year AI contracts

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Large US cloud server procurement growth returns above 5% quarter over quarter with accelerator-led servers taking a rising share for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Agent workloads spend much of their time on ordinary computing and data handling rather than on model maths, so the mix of servers bought shifts with them.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the slowdown reflects workload mix or simply parts shortages; all three findings come from one publisher.
entries.statement: Cloud providers are shifting part of their new server buying away from accelerator-heavy machines toward ordinary processors and storage as agent-style work spreads.
entries.title: Agent-style workloads tilt cloud buying toward general-purpose servers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Next-generation rack quotes settle below $4 million per unit, or quoted rack prices fall for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Each generation adds more memory, power and networking content, and scarcity lets the vendor price that content at a premium.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory prices, which drive most of the added content cost; all three findings come from one publisher.
entries.statement: Buyers are being quoted about twice as much for the next generation of AI racks as for the current one, so the price of a unit of leading-edge capacity is rising sharply between generations.
entries.title: Each new rack generation lands at roughly twice the price of the last

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No named customer reports running two vendors' rack systems in one production cluster within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors design their systems to hand work to each other, which lowers the cost of adding a second brand inside one cluster.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the interoperability shown in launch material appears in real deployments.
entries.statement: Buyers are beginning to run machines from competing vendors side by side inside a single cluster, with each vendor's system designed to hand work to the others.
entries.title: Clusters start mixing hardware from rival vendors

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No AI hardware supplier raises new equity or debt above $1 billion for capacity or customer financing for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Capacity has to be paid for before the revenue it will carry arrives, so suppliers raise outside money rather than wait for earnings.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to equity and credit market conditions for semiconductor issuers.
entries.statement: The companies selling AI hardware are themselves issuing shares and bonds to pay for the capacity they need, rather than funding it from what they earn.
entries.title: Chip suppliers now raise outside money to fund their own expansion

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The second design partner books no custom-silicon revenue from this buyer within 4 quarters, or the agreement lapses within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Adding a second design partner protects the buyer's chip roadmap from any single supplier's delays and gives it more bargaining power on price.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the warrant tranches actually vest against delivered revenue; all three findings come from one publisher.
entries.statement: One of the biggest in-house chip programmes has added a second outside design partner alongside its incumbent, so even custom silicon now gets second-sourced.
entries.title: A large buyer adds a second designer for its own chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A named plant tied to public support is cancelled or delayed past 2028 when the support does not arrive, or 2 consecutive quarters pass with no new government-backed AI capacity announcement.
entries.mechanism: When a plant only proceeds if public support arrives, the state's decision rather than the market sets the pace of new supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the promised public support is actually appropriated.
entries.statement: The largest new chip, memory and packaging plants are being announced with public support attached, so state backing now decides how fast supply grows.
entries.title: Government money underwrites the next wave of AI supply

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new chip supply agreement carrying customer warrants is disclosed for 2 consecutive quarters, or a disclosed warrant fails to vest against its first purchase milestone.
entries.mechanism: Paying part of the price in warrants lets the buyer conserve cash and ties the supplier's reward to hitting purchase milestones rather than to the sale itself.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the buyers' share prices, which set what the warrants are worth.
entries.statement: Large customers are attaching share warrants tied to purchase milestones to their chip agreements, so suppliers take part of their reward in the buyer's stock rather than in cash.
entries.title: Big buyers now pay their chip suppliers in share warrants

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Mediation concludes with a settlement and no strike vote is called within 2 quarters, or the rejected wage agreement is ratified within 1 quarter.
entries.mechanism: Memory is already the tightest input in the AI server, so an interruption at a plant carrying a large share of one supplier's output feeds straight through to how many accelerators can be finished.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the September 2026 mediation outcome and to whether any stoppage touches lines making stacked memory rather than ordinary memory.
entries.statement: Union action at the memory makers has become a live risk to memory output, with a Taiwanese workforce moving toward a strike and a Korean union narrowly rejecting its wage deal.
entries.title: Labour disputes reach the memory suppliers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No tariff rule covering finished data-centre servers is published with a rate and effective date within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A tariff applied to the assembled server rather than the chip alone would raise the landed cost of every imported rack and reward the vendors that have already committed to building in the United States.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the allowance mechanism survives into the final rule, since that determines which suppliers absorb the cost.
entries.statement: Washington is preparing semiconductor tariffs that would extend to finished data-centre servers, with duty-free import allowances sized to each company's US chip-fabrication investment, though no rate or start date has been set.
entries.title: Tariffs on finished AI hardware become a new policy risk

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA discloses new commitments under the compute-partnership programme above $36 billion within 2 quarters, or a regulator opens a formal inquiry into it within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: If the vendor pulls back on credit support, the smaller cloud providers that relied on it have to fund purchases themselves, which slows the orders that support drew forward.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the reported pause is confirmed by a primary disclosure, since the vendor denies it.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's compute-partnership financing programme has run into internal antitrust concerns and partner objections, and reporting says some deals have been paused, which NVIDIA denies.
entries.title: The vendor financing programme draws internal and partner pushback
